findings.summary: The "Golden rule" callout teaches quoting of `"$@"` on page 1, but `$@` and positional parameters are not introduced until page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 ends with: `{"type":"callout","style":"tip","title":"Golden rule","text":"Always write `\"$@\"` with quotes. Bare `$@` word-splits and glob-expands every argument you were handed."}` — page 2 is where `$@` is first defined: "`$#` = count of args passed to the function" and the table row "`\"$@\"` | N quoted words".
findings.fix: Move the Golden-rule callout to page 2, directly after the "`$@` versus `$*`" table, where the reader has just seen the three expansion forms.

findings.summary: The positional-parameter diagram at the top right renders as misaligned cells that overflow and overlap the row and its index labels.
findings.evidence: The cells `$0 script`, `$1 Bob`, `$2 42`, `$# 2` and `$@ Bob 42` sit at three different vertical offsets: the `$# 2` cell drops below the row baseline while the `$@ Bob 42` cell extends above the row top into the `3`/`4` index labels, and the word `script` touches both side borders of its cell.
findings.fix: Give every cell in the parameter-slot diagram a single shared baseline and uniform height, and pad the cells so the longest label (`script`) clears the box borders.

findings.summary: `local` is used in the argument examples on page 2 and is the subject of a full gotcha section on page 3, but is not defined until page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "local name=\"${1:-anon}\"   # unset OR empty", "local f=\"${1:?path required}\"", "read_cfg() { local -n out=$1; out=loaded; }". Page 4 is the first definition: "`local x` covers the function and everything it calls" / "The previous value is restored when the function returns".
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss to page 2 before the "Defaults and Guards" code (e.g. "`local` confines a variable to this call — full rules on the scope page"), or move the page-4 "Dynamic, Not Lexical" bullets ahead of the argument defaults.

findings.summary: The `local x=$(cmd)` status-eater section appears before command substitution is introduced later on the same page.
findings.evidence: The "The `local` Status Eater" block — "local x=$(cmd)        # status is local's: 0" — precedes "Data Leaves via stdout", which is where `$( )` is first explained: "A function 'returns' data by WRITING it to stdout" / "Caller captures with `result=$(f)`".
findings.fix: Reorder page 3 so "Data Leaves via stdout" (and the `result=$(f)` capture) comes before "The `local` Status Eater", which is a gotcha about that construct.

findings.summary: The whole Output page rests on subshell semantics that are only defined on page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 4 opens with `{"type":"diagram","kind":"flow","spec":{"nodes":["caller","fork subshell","f runs","stdout back","vars lost"]}}` and later asserts "A pipe puts `mapfile` in a subshell — array vanishes" and "`f | while read ...` runs the `while` in a subshell under Bash defaults". The definition arrives on page 5: "A forked copy of the shell process" / "Inherits all state; nothing it changes flows back".
findings.fix: Move the page-5 "Definition" bullets and the "Forks / Does not" cards to the top of page 4, before "Capture Forks", so the reader knows what a subshell is the first time capture, `mapfile` and pipelines depend on it.

findings.summary: The page 4 title "Output: The Data Channel" describes only the first half of the page, whose final third covers dynamic scope and `local` declarations instead.
findings.evidence: Page 4 (`page_title: "Output: The Data Channel"`) ends with the headings "Dynamic, Not Lexical" ("A callee SEES the caller's locals — and can modify them", "`local x` covers the function and everything it calls"), a scope flowchart titled "main: local tmp", and "Declaring" ("local a b c  # three locals") — material the next page's title, "Locals, Scope and What a Subshell Is", claims.
findings.fix: Retitle page 4 to cover both halves, e.g. "Output, Then Dynamic Scope" — or move the "Dynamic, Not Lexical", scope-flowchart and "Declaring" blocks onto page 5 (which currently opens cold on a `local` flags table with no heading) and keep the existing title.

findings.summary: Page 6 ends with a `trap ... EXIT` cleanup pattern and discusses `ERR`/`RETURN` trap inheritance before traps are introduced on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6: "Without `-E`, `ERR` traps skip functions and `$( )`", "`set -T` (functrace) does the same for `RETURN` and `DEBUG`", and the closing code "trap 'rm -rf \"$tmp\"' EXIT   # set it NOW". Page 7 is titled "Traps: EXIT, ERR and Clean Exits" and only there does the table state "`EXIT` | shell exits | —" and "`ERR` | command fails | `set -E` to inherit".
findings.fix: Move the `-E`/`-T` bullets and the `mktemp`/`trap ... EXIT` cleanup code to page 7, after the trap table, and let page 6 end on the strict header.

findings.summary: The "Skeleton to Memorise" prints `$out`, a variable the skeleton never assigns or declares, so the example does not demonstrate the contract it teaches.
findings.evidence: "f() {", "  local a=\"${1:?}\" b=\"${2:-default}\"", "  printf '%s\\n' \"$out\"", "  return 0", "}" — `out` appears from nowhere, and page 5 has just told the reader "`set -u` turns unset reads into hard errors".
findings.fix: Restore a body line that produces the value, e.g. `local out; out=$(work "$a" "$b") || return 1` before the `printf`, so the skeleton is runnable under `set -u`.

findings.summary: The "Ans→" marker under each question heading renders far too small to read.
findings.evidence: On pages 2, 5 and 7 a roughly 4px-tall "Ans→" label appears beneath the headings "Why did f my file.txt see two arguments?", "Why does local fail at the top of my script?" and "Why did my ERR trap stay silent?".
findings.fix: Raise the answer-marker font size to the body minimum (or drop the marker entirely, since the answer bullets follow it directly).

findings.summary: `main() { setup; run "$@"; }` is dropped on page 1 with no explanation; the reason for the pattern is on pages 9 and 10.
findings.evidence: Page 1 code block: "main() { setup; run \"$@\"; }" / "main \"$@\"     # last line of the file" sits between the "Core idea" takeaway and the Golden-rule callout with no heading or bullets. The rationale only appears on page 9 ("Define functions at the top, or wrap in `main` called last" / "A straight-line script runs definitions in order — nothing hoists") and page 10.
findings.fix: Either delete the block from page 1 or attach it to page 1's "Definition is a runtime act" bullet with the one-line reason ("definitions run in order — nothing hoists").

findings.summary: "Subshell" is used as a load-bearing term on page 1 but is not defined until page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 1: heading "Parens Make a Subshell" with "work() ( cd /tmp; make )  # body IS a subshell". Page 5: "Definition — A forked copy of the shell process".
findings.fix: Add a half-line gloss at the page-1 use ("a subshell is a forked copy of the shell — details on the scope page") so the `( )` form is meaningful on first contact.

findings.summary: `die` is called in the `$?` example on page 2 but is not defined until page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "(( rc == 2 )) && die 'bad input'". Page 8 defines it: "die() { printf '%s\\n' \"$*\" >&2; exit 1; }".
findings.fix: Replace `die 'bad input'` with an inline `printf ... >&2; return 2` on page 2, or add a one-line "`die` = print to stderr and exit; defined later" note.

findings.summary: `IFS` is referenced as the joining character for `"$*"` but is never expanded or defined anywhere in the handbook.
findings.evidence: Page 2 table row: "`\"$*\"` | one word, joined by `IFS[0]`". The only other mention is page 6's "IFS=$'\\n\\t'   # no space-splitting", which also assumes the reader knows the variable.
findings.fix: Expand on first use: "joined by the first character of `IFS` (the field separator, a space by default)".

findings.summary: The claim that `echo` "eats backslashes" is false for Bash's builtin `echo` under default settings, where backslash escapes are only interpreted with `-e` or `xpg_echo`.
findings.evidence: Page 4: "`echo` mangles a leading `-` and eats backslashes"; repeated on page 9: "`echo` for data mangles `-n` and backslashes". In Bash, `echo 'a\tb'` prints `a\tb` literally unless `-e` is given or `shopt -s xpg_echo` is set.
findings.fix: Reword to the portability-accurate version, e.g. "`echo` swallows leading `-n`/`-e`/`-E`, and backslash handling varies by shell and build (`dash`/`sh`, or Bash with `xpg_echo`, expand `\t`) — so use `printf '%s\n'`."

findings.summary: Heading "Definition" already appears on page 1.
findings.evidence: Definition
findings.fix: Fine if the two pages cover different topics; rename if they do not.

findings.summary: The counterintuitive claim that `unset` inside a function can remove the caller's variable is asserted with no example, unlike every other scope rule on the page.
findings.evidence: Page 5 bullet: "`unset x` inside can unset the CALLER's variable" — no code block accompanies it, while the neighbouring nameref rule gets a three-line example.
findings.fix: Add a two-line example showing the caller's value re-exposed, e.g. `x=outer; f() { local x=inner; unset x; echo "$x"; }; f` printing `outer`.

findings.summary: The pinned sticky note overlaps the closing comment line of the trap code block.
findings.evidence: The pin for the note "save $? on the trap's first command" overlaps the comment line `# a bare exit would reset it to 0`.
findings.fix: Move the note's anchor point below the final comment line, or reserve vertical space in the code block for the pinned note.

findings.summary: The FUNCNAME stack diagram puts `main` at index 2 and `source` at index 3, but bash always places `main` at the highest index.
findings.evidence: Diagram captioned "FUNCNAME" with cells `[0] fact`, `[1] compute`, `[2] main`, `[3] source`; the Bash Reference Manual states of FUNCNAME: "The bottom-most element (the one with the highest index) is \"main\"."
findings.fix: Swap the last two cells so the stack reads `[0] fact`, `[1] compute`, `[2] source`, `[3] main` (a `source` frame appears below the function frames but above `main`, never after it).

findings.summary: The Common Mistakes page opens with a cross-process sidebox that belongs to the previous page's topic, and the same point is repeated later on the page.
findings.evidence: Page 9's first block, before any heading, is `{"type":"sidebox","title":"Crossing processes","items":["`export -f f` then `bash -c 'f'` works","`find -exec` needs `bash -c` for the same reason","Exec'd binaries cannot see shell functions"]}`; later the same page repeats "`export -f` is Bash-to-Bash only — python children see nothing" in the "Two false hopes" sidebox.
findings.fix: Move the "Crossing processes" sidebox back to page 8 next to "Nesting and Sourcing", and leave the export-f limitation on page 9 only inside "Two false hopes".

findings.summary: The portability table labels the `function` keyword and arrays/`[[ ]]` as "Bash only" when all three originate in ksh and are also supported by ksh93 and zsh.
findings.evidence: Table "Feature | Portable?" rows: "`function` keyword | Bash only" and "arrays, `[[ ]]` | Bash only" — while the adjacent row correctly phrases `local` as "not POSIX, universal".
findings.fix: Change both answers to "not POSIX (bash/ksh/zsh)", matching the phrasing already used for `local`, since the practical warning is that `dash`/POSIX `sh` rejects them, not that ksh and zsh lack them.

findings.summary: The pinned sticky note overlaps the last line of the adjacent code block.
findings.evidence: The pin and top edge of the note "copy it before anything else runs" sit on top of the code line `(( rc == 0 )) || die 'backup'`.
findings.fix: Offset the sticky note below the code block's last line (or add bottom padding to the code block) so the note and pin do not land on `die 'backup'`.
